question: A monitoring script sizes tables by running `ls -l` on the path returned by `pg_relation_filepath`. For one busy table it has reported exactly 1073741824 bytes for weeks, while the row count keeps climbing and disk keeps filling. Before touching the database, what should the engineer conclude about the script?
choices: One gigabyte is the per-relation size limit the server enforces on the main file; once it is reached, further rows are diverted into the table's TOAST relation. The script is reporting the main file correctly and only needs to add the TOAST relation's size to it

It is measuring one segment. Past 1 GB a relation's file is cut into gigabyte segments — `16986`, `16986.1`, `16986.2`, … — so the base file pins at exactly 1 GB forever while growth continues in its siblings; the script also never sees the `_fsm` and `_vm` forks, which are separate files beside the main one. Size is a question for `pg_relation_size` / `pg_total_relation_size`, which sum segments, forks and TOAST

The file is a pre-allocated extent: PostgreSQL reserves space in powers of two and appends rows inside the reservation until it fills, then allocates a larger one. A flat 1 GB means the current extent is exactly full, and the script is stale because the relation has since been moved to a new, larger file

The script is following a stale `relfilenode`. Each checkpoint writes the relation out to a fresh file number and leaves the previous file behind untouched, so the script has been sizing an orphan since the last checkpoint; resolving `pg_class.relfilenode` on every run fixes it
explanation: A relation is an ordinary file, but not necessarily one file. To stay clear of platform file-size limits, PostgreSQL cuts a relation at 1 GB and continues in numbered segments — `16986`, `16986.1`, and so on — so a file frozen at exactly 2^30 bytes is the signature of segmentation, not of a table that stopped growing. Two more things live outside that file: the free space map (`_fsm`) and visibility map (`_vm`) forks, each its own file, and any TOASTed values, which live in a separate companion relation with its own file and index. This is exactly why size questions belong to `pg_relation_size` (main fork, all segments) and `pg_total_relation_size` (plus forks, TOAST and indexes) rather than to the file system. The distractors each invent a mechanism PostgreSQL does not have: there is no 1 GB relation limit (TOAST is triggered by tuple width, ~2 KB, not by file size), no power-of-two extent reservation (the file grows one 8 KB page at a time), and checkpoints never renumber a relation — `relfilenode` does change, but on rewrites such as VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER or TRUNCATE, not on a routine checkpoint.

question: In a design review, someone proposes a "zero-indirection" heap: index entries and row addresses would carry a tuple's byte offset within its page directly, skipping the line-pointer array — one less dereference per lookup and 4 bytes saved per row. What does the slotted-page design buy that this proposal gives up?
choices: Cross-page addressing. A raw byte offset could only address within a single page, so a relation would be capped at one page of addressable rows; the slot array is what makes an address a `(page, slot)` pair instead of a single number, and it is also what lets a tuple spill across a page boundary when a value is wide

Alignment freedom. Slots let tuples start at arbitrary byte offsets while everything that points at them addresses fixed-size units; without the indirection, every tuple would have to be padded up to a multiple of 8 bytes, costing far more than the 4 bytes the proposal saves

Concurrency. The 4-byte slot is the unit a writer locks while modifying a row, so direct offsets would force an exclusive lock on the whole page for every update, and `pd_lower`/`pd_upper` would stop being maintainable because free space could no longer be computed as a single subtraction

The freedom to move a tuple without touching anything that points at it. An address names the slot, and the slot holds the tuple's current offset — so a page can slide its tuples together to reclaim the gaps left by dead rows while every existing address stays valid, with no index update at all. The slot is also a small state machine — unused, normal, dead, redirect — and the redirect state is what lets an old address keep resolving after the version it originally named was replaced
explanation: The line pointer is not an accident of layout; it is the one level of indirection that makes intra-page maintenance cheap. Because a `ctid` names the slot rather than the bytes, page-level cleanup can compact tuples toward the end of the page, moving them physically, without invalidating a single index entry — under the proposal, every such compaction would require rewriting every index that points into that page, which is precisely the cost the design exists to avoid. The slot's state bits matter just as much: `lp_flags` distinguishes unused, normal, dead and redirect, and the redirect state is what lets address `(7,2)` keep resolving to a live tuple that now sits in slot 5. Strip the slot and both the relocation and the forwarding disappear. The distractors misattribute the mechanism. Alignment padding is decided by the tuple's own layout and happens with or without slots. Row-level locking lives in the tuple header (`t_xmax` and the info-mask bits), not in the line pointer, and `pd_lower`/`pd_upper` bound the free space precisely because the slot array grows forward from the header while tuples grow backward from the end. And addressing beyond one page is handled by the page number in the `(page, slot)` pair either way — a tuple can never span pages, which is exactly why TOAST exists.

question: A service caches each row's `ctid` in an external key-value store as a fast handle for later lookups, reasoning that the line-pointer indirection means an address survives the tuple moving. Six months in, some lookups quietly return the wrong row's data. What is the flaw in the original reasoning?
choices: The indirection is intra-page and version-scoped, not an identity. It survives a tuple sliding within its own page, and a redirect slot can keep an old address resolving for a while; it does not survive an update that writes the new version onto another page, and VACUUM FULL or CLUSTER rewrite the whole relation and reassign every address. Worse than going stale, an address can be recycled: once cleanup frees a slot, a later insert reuses that same `(page, slot)`, so the cached handle silently resolves to an unrelated row

The handle is only unstable across server restarts. `ctid` is an in-memory address the buffer manager assigns when a page is faulted in, so it is stable for the lifetime of the running instance and the cache simply needs to be invalidated on restart

It is safe for reads and unsafe only for writes. A `SELECT … WHERE ctid = …` follows `t_ctid` forward along the version chain and therefore always lands on the current version, so the cache self-heals on read; only a `DELETE`/`UPDATE` addressed by `ctid` risks acting on a stale version

The reasoning holds for the row itself; the exposure is confined to wide columns. TOASTed values are chunked into a separate relation whose chunks are relocated independently of the main tuple, so the cached `ctid` still names the right row but may reassemble a stale payload for the oversized attributes
explanation: `ctid` is an address, not an identity — a `(page, slot)` pair that says where a row version can be found right now. The indirection through the line pointer buys exactly one guarantee: the tuple's bytes may move inside its page and the address still resolves. Everything else moves the address. An update writes a new version, and unless it can stay on the same page it lands at a different `(page, slot)`; VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER rewrite the entire relation and renumber everything. The failure mode that produces wrong data rather than a miss is slot recycling: after cleanup marks a line pointer unused, a subsequent insert can claim that slot, so a long-lived cached address ends up pointing at a live, unrelated row with no error raised anywhere. That silence is why a stable key must be a value in the row — a primary key — not a physical address. The distractors each dress up a plausible-sounding stability claim: `ctid` is on-disk, not a buffer-manager artifact, so restarts are irrelevant; `t_ctid` chains are followed by MVCC and HOT logic during scans, not by a literal `WHERE ctid = …` predicate, which resolves one slot and stops; and TOAST chunks are reached through the 18-byte pointer stored in the tuple, so they are as current as the tuple version that holds them.

question: To stop background I/O during business hours, a team disables autovacuum on an update-heavy table and schedules a manual VACUUM every night. They budget the cost as "dead row versions linger for up to a day, then get cleaned up." Which second-order cost does this Sheet's model of the heap predict they have missed?
choices: Pages stop accepting new tuples. With no cleanup, dead tuples are never removed, so `pd_upper` never moves back down the page and each page becomes permanently unable to fit another row — the table degrades toward one live row per page until the nightly run

Tuple headers inflate. Every dead version accumulates `t_xmax` and info-mask state that grows the 23-byte header, so the day's rows are progressively wider on disk and the nightly VACUUM has to rewrite each page to shrink them back

The forks beside the main file go stale too. The free space map is maintained mainly by VACUUM, so the space that the day's dead rows free is never recorded — inserts and new row versions cannot find it, and the relation extends with fresh pages instead of reusing what it already has. The day's bloat therefore compounds into permanent file growth rather than being merely deferred, and the visibility map's all-visible bits, which only VACUUM sets and any write clears, stay cleared all day

There is no second-order cost on the storage side. Free space is recorded in the FSM by the backend that deletes or supersedes the row, so it is discoverable immediately; the only thing that lags is the visibility map, and that is a planner concern rather than a space one
explanation: A heap has no order, so "where is there room?" is not a question the main file can answer — it is answered by the free space map fork, one byte per heap page, arranged as a tree whose upper levels hold the maximum of their children so a lookup costs a few page reads instead of a scan. That fork is kept approximately current mainly by VACUUM. Suspend VACUUM and the freed space still physically exists but becomes invisible to the code that places new tuples, so the relation extends with brand-new pages while old ones sit half empty. That is the trap in the team's budget: the cost is not "dead rows linger for a day", it is a file that grows and does not shrink back, since a heap reuses space in place and rarely returns it to the file system. The visibility map degrades in the same window — its all-visible bit is set only by VACUUM and cleared by any write to the page, so a day of updates leaves it uniformly cleared. The distractors invert the mechanism: pages do reclaim space, but only when cleanup runs; tuple headers are fixed at 23 bytes plus an optional null bitmap and never grow with transaction activity; and treating the FSM as eagerly maintained by the deleting backend is exactly the assumption that makes disabling VACUUM look free.

question: A table carries a `payload jsonb` column averaging 2 MB per row alongside a dozen narrow columns. Reporting queries select only the narrow columns and run slowly, so an engineer proposes splitting `payload` into a side table joined on id, expecting the scans to stop dragging megabytes per row through the buffer pool. How should the proposal be judged against this Sheet's storage model?
choices: The expectation is sound: TOAST keeps compressed values inline as long as they fit, so up to 8 KB of `payload` rides along in every tuple the reporting scan reads. Only above one page's worth does storage go out-of-line, and the split is what guarantees the narrow scan never carries the payload

The expectation is sound for a different reason: TOAST pointers are resolved when a tuple is deserialised, regardless of the SELECT list, so every scanned row already pays one TOAST-table lookup. Declaring the column `EXTERNAL` would achieve the same thing as the split without schema surgery

The expectation is unfounded and so is the premise: past ~2 KB TOAST switches the row to `PLAIN` storage inside the TOAST table, so the main relation already holds little more than ids and the reporting scan is reading a narrow table. Any slowness must come from reassembling chunks for the id column

The heap has already performed that split. Past roughly 2 KB, TOAST compresses the wide values and then moves the widest out into the table's companion TOAST relation in ~2 KB chunks, leaving an 18-byte pointer in the main tuple whatever the value's true size — and the chunks are fetched only when a query actually selects that column. The reporting scan is therefore already reading narrow tuples; a manual side table largely reimplements the TOAST table by hand, and the real cause of the slowness has to be looked for elsewhere
explanation: TOAST exists because a tuple cannot span pages and the system wants at least four tuples per page, so a row heading past ~2 KB is shrunk: compress the wide variable-length values first, then push the widest out-of-line into the companion TOAST relation as ~2 KB chunks, leaving an 18-byte pointer behind. Two consequences decide this design review. First, the main tuple's width is bounded no matter how large the value is, so a sequential scan over narrow columns reads narrow pages. Second, chunk retrieval is lazy — it happens only when the query actually selects the TOASTed column — so the reporting queries never touch the 2 MB at all. The proposed side table is therefore mostly a hand-rolled duplicate of a table PostgreSQL already created, and the investigation should move to what the scan really pays for: page count of the narrow tuples, missing indexes, or the per-column strategy (`EXTENDED`, `EXTERNAL`, `MAIN`, `PLAIN`) if inline compression is genuinely hurting. The distractors each break a specific rule: values do not stay inline up to 8 KB, the ~2 KB threshold and the four-tuples-per-page goal set the budget; pointers are not dereferenced eagerly, which is the whole point of the 18-byte stub; and `PLAIN` means neither compressed nor moved out-of-line, so it is the one strategy that could never apply to an oversized value.
